chapters.en: Last time, we left the Battle of Messina in its middle phase. At first contact, the player's side had 1,288 men and the enemy had 330. That difference looks like a simple sum, but a war is not settled by the starting headcount. More enemy troops entered, knights could be wounded or killed, and the wounded on the field still faced pursuit and the final reckoning. Today we will open four ledgers from the second half of this battle: whose soft casualties became hard losses, who disappeared from the knight roster, how a new army changed combat width, and how victory or defeat entered the war score. Before we begin, a word about the source labels that will recur on screen. These readings come from checkpoints on different dates in the same Messina battle case and from several independent vanilla CK3 replays. They share a battle identity, but they need not share each day's random outcomes. We trace causes only between states within one replay. Whenever we switch replays, the picture will say so. The same CombatID does not turn two different trajectories into one continuous recording.

We now enter independent replay 004. On day 28, the battle has moved from its main phase into pursuit. The whole numbers on screen can hide a crucial distinction: current fighters, recoverable soft casualties, and losses already recorded as hard casualties occupy different columns. Pursuit does not simply deal another round of main-phase damage. It works through the losing side's existing soft-casualty pool and determines how much of that pool becomes hard loss. We freeze the vanilla state on day 28 and ask whether that frame's pursuit, toughness, soft-casualty, and screen inputs can carry the calculation through day 31. Look at the losing side's 24 regiments. The winner's daily pursuit-damage value is 75,203,000 raw units, and the losing side's aggregate effective screen is zero in this replay. The engine first forms two available budgets and distributes them in regiment order: it allocates the evenly divisible proportional shares, then handles the remainders left by integer truncation. It does not hand every regiment an arbitrary equal loss, and we have not captured a pursuit lottery here. The calculation card shows both raw integers and the values divided by 100,000. A Q100000 value above 75 million does not mean more than 75 million people. The first turn of the page runs from day 28 to day 29. The soft-casualty changes for all 24 regiments match the next vanilla frame, as do the 23 hard-casualty entries that the game exposes for comparison. On that day, 2,070,677 raw units move from soft to hard loss, equivalent to 20.70677 people. One non-main regiment has a null hard-casualty field in the vanilla readback. Null is not zero, so we report zero difference only for the 23 entries that can actually be compared. The second day continues from the same day-28 starting state. We do not feed the losing side's day-29 answer back into the model. From day 29 to day 30, all 24 soft entries and 23 readable hard entries again have zero difference, with 20.97473 additional people-equivalent in hard loss. From day 30 to day 31, the same 24 and 23 comparisons have zero difference, and hard loss grows by another 21.26119 people-equivalent. Across three days, that is 62.94269 people-equivalent: 72 soft-casualty changes and 69 readable hard-casualty changes all agree. Why do the daily losses differ? The winner's raw pursuit-damage value stays at 75,203,000 on all three days, but the losing side's soft-casualty pool shrinks. The relevant toughness and budgets must be recalculated each day. Multiplying the first day's answer by three misses that change. Meanwhile, current fighting strength stays unchanged for the comparable regiments. Pursuit is changing the casualty ledger; a large unchanged headcount on the battle screen does not show that no new losses occurred. This result has a narrow scope, and that is what makes it useful. Given the vanilla day-28 state in this replay, we can calculate three days of regiment-level soft and hard casualties with zero difference. It does not show that the losing side's screen is zero in every battle. A nonzero screen takes the budget into a branch for which we have no same-frame vanilla regiment sample. We will not present a static test vector as a filmed vanilla battle. Nor have we predicted the whole battle's win probability from its pre-battle state.

Let us step back from pursuit to day 5, because one ledger entry does not appear in regiment headcounts. In the pre-event save of independent replay 039, knight 34333 has not yet received this injury. After the vanilla event runs that day, he survives but is maimed, losing a leg, and has a minor wound. His opponent, character 47032, gains 150 prestige. Item zero, selected from this event's growth list, does not raise that opponent's base prowess. Do not combine this new maiming event with an older injury report already present in the source save. Battle-report lists accumulate entries; only the before-and-after difference tells us what happened that day. The knight is still there, but the next combat input has changed. Read-only replay 040 does not advance the date again. It loads the day-6 state saved by 039 byte for byte, then asks vanilla CK3 for the next paused frame that the playing agent would consume. The knight remains in the roster of 24, and regiment 61 still contains one person. Yet his effective prowess falls from 11 to 7, while knight effectiveness remains 1.75. At the old effective value, damage is 11 times 1.75 times 50, or 962.5. At the new value, 7 times 1.75 times 50 gives 612.5. Toughness likewise falls from 192.5 to 122.5. His base prowess did not fall by four points; the injury changed the effective value read on the next frame. A character event that barely shows up in the map headcount has therefore entered the next combat calculation. We are describing this one knight and this one frame. Ordinary daily casualties in other regiments may also change, so not every before-and-after difference can be blamed on this maiming. Nor can we announce a later treatment result in a day-6 frame. The next source is another day-26 replay, labelled 020. Its vanilla event table selects knight_killed. The opponent selector begins with 19 knights. After the event's prowess threshold, 14 are eligible for the draw. The engine selects without weights. Its local random value here is 1,400,813,912; divided by 14, the remainder is eight. When the native candidate container removes an ineligible entry, it fills the gap with the last item and checks the current index again. In that order, candidate eight is character 34120. Keeping ordinary spreadsheet order after deletion would point the same index at someone else. The newly added vanilla battle report names 34120 as the killer. The selected victim is character 33437, tied to regiment 65. At one event boundary he is still in the battle. At the next, he has a death marker and the character-to-regiment link has been cleared. The later save records death in battle and names 34120 as killer. The killer gains 150 in prestige currency and 150 in accumulated prestige. Another detail matters: the victim's base prowess is two in both saves. The core native reading that falls from four to two is effective prowess. Calling this a two-point loss of base prowess would read the wrong ledger. We also have independent replay 070, started separately from the same day-26 source save. It reads the killer's actual runtime growth-list weights as 40, 30, and 15. The actual list draw is 51,510,340, with threshold two; it lands on item zero, which grants no prowess. The day-27 roster comes from another post-event save chain. Run 036 saves its immutable post-event state, and run 038 reloads those exact bytes. On the next paused frame, the roster falls from 69 to 68 regiments and from 30 to 29 knights. The missing entries are character 33437 and regiment 65. The selector in 020, the growth weights in 070, and the roster in 036 to 038 each have their own receipts. They help explain one another, but 038 cannot be passed off as the direct next frame of 020 or 070. These two outcomes sketch the shape of character risk. The maimed knight stays in battle with weaker attributes. The killed knight leaves the roster, while his opponent receives prestige. They are not a complete table of injury, treatment, and death probabilities. To place character risk into a full battle distribution, we would still need to verify other event branches, conditional weights, writeback, and future daily refreshes. Today, each observed character chain stays on its own source card.

We return to pursuit replay 004. Its vanilla day-32 terminal record says normal_result, with combat side zero as winner. The player's army 18 leaves the old CombatID and enters a retreating state after defeat. Be careful with the word attacker: in this battle, side zero attacks and belongs to the enemy, while the player attacks in the war. Reading winner equals zero as a player victory would swap the columns of two different ledgers. The retreat that follows a normal terminal result is not evidence that the war AI ordered a withdrawal during combat. How does the battle enter the war score? We cold-load the day-27 checkpoint created within run 004 and start a separate replay, A05. It keeps the battle and war identities, but it is not a seamless continuation of 004's random trajectory. On day 32, A05 obtains a new native battle-score writer receipt and pairs the written result with the native paused WarID 4 state from that same replay. The matching numbers in old run 024 remain only an independent historical comparison. We cannot derive the formula by staring at minus 50. We start with the integers that the A05 writer actually read. The losing combat side has a starting baseline of 129,800,000 raw units, equivalent to 1,298 people. A05's stored terminal current value is zero; levy soft casualties are 57,753,614 and men-at-arms soft casualties are 18,384,344. Subtracting in the vanilla integer order gives a hard-loss numerator of 53,662,042 raw units, or 536.62042 people-equivalent. All four inputs come from the same A05 native writer call, not from the war total displayed on screen. Now the denominator. In this A05 writer call, vanilla CK3 reads eight military buckets for the losing war participant, Robert: zero, 675, 310, zero, zero, zero, 11, zero. Together they make 996 people. The 1,298 figure is the starting baseline for this combat side. The 996 figure is the war-participant denominator used for this battle-score ratio. Substituting the former for the latter changes every following step. Vanilla integer division first gives 53,662,042 divided by 996 equals 53,877, or 53.877 percent after scaling. The defender-victory battle-score coefficient loaded for A05's casus belli is 15,000,000 raw units, or 150 war-score points after scaling. The next integer multiplication and division gives an uncapped value of 8,081,550 raw units, or 80.8155 points. Under the stock rule for this game version, one battle is capped at 50. A05's writer records a positive 50 for this battle row. The positive sign belongs to the winning war defender. From the player's position as war attacker, the writer's relative battle row is minus 50. A separate native paused snapshot from day 32 of the same A05 replay records the total war score as minus 50. The two sources support each other, but the later total alone cannot establish the numerator and denominator before the cap. This calculation closes the local writer and same-run war state for A05's normal battle end. It does not show that every casus belli uses the same coefficient, or that we have measured other peace effects, legitimacy changes, or the AI's next decision. A05's army 18 enters a post-defeat retreating state. That is a terminal result, not an active withdrawal order issued by the war AI during combat. The calculation card leaves one firm conclusion for this battle: the terminal result enters the war ledger with the correct attacker and defender identities.

Across these independent Messina replays, the second half of the battle shows at least four different kinds of change. Pursuit in 004 converts existing soft casualties into hard losses. Knight events in 039 and 036 change character states, which then change attributes or roster entries in their respective next frames. Reinforcement in 085 changes participants, cached totals, and combat width. A05, cold-loaded separately from the day-27 checkpoint made within 004, puts the native writer for a normal terminal result and the native paused war state into the same new replay. A single battle icon on the map cannot show the order of these ledgers. We only know which steps have been accounted for when we put every vanilla input, transition, and result back on its own timeline. Several doors remain closed: a naturally observed battle with nonzero screen for the losing side; the precise route and arrival date of future reinforcements; an active withdrawal by the ordinary AI during combat; the full writeback for other knight events; and calibration of a whole-battle probability across different conditions. This episode presents several calculable mechanisms in vanilla replays with the same battle identity. It does not present the vanilla whole-battle win probability for this position. Next time, the useful question is not which percentage to stick on this defeat. It is whether these ledgers still reconcile when the conditions change.
